questions.learningObjective: Trim a wordy connector

stimulus.body: The astronomer writes: 'In the event that clouds appear, we will stop.'

questions.stem: Which revision is most concise?

options.text: 'In the event that clouds appear, we stop.'
'In the event that clouds appear, we will stop tonight.'
'If clouds appear, we will stop.'
'Clouds appearing means we stop.'

questions.explanation: 'In the event that' is a wordy substitute for 'if'. Replacing it cuts four words with no loss.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Spot a nominalised action
questions.stem: An astronomer writes 'There was a recording of the spectrum by the team.' Which nominalisation is present?

options.text: 'There was' is the only problem.
'spectrum' is too technical.
'team' hides the individual.
'recording' turns 'recorded' into a noun.

questions.explanation: 'Recording' buries the verb. 'The team recorded the spectrum' is direct and clear.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Choose voice for an equipment manual
questions.stem: An equipment manual should show who calibrates the sensor. Which voice fits?

options.text: Passive voice to sound formal.
Active voice naming the calibrator.
Imperative mood with no actor.
Question form throughout.

questions.explanation: Active voice names who calibrates, which aids accountability and troubleshooting.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Replace empty hedges with data
questions.stem: An astronomer logs 'perhaps the seeing was good, maybe.' How should the hedging be fixed?

answer.exemplar: Replace the empty hedges with one qualifier tied to a measured seeing value, such as 'seeing averaged 2.3 arcseconds.'

questions.explanation: Multiple empty hedges add no information. A single qualifier backed by a measurement communicates real uncertainty.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Supply a base for a percentage claim

stimulus.body: The log claims 'temperature fell 10% overnight.'

questions.stem: What would make this claim checkable?

options.text: The observer's name.
The thermometer brand.
The starting temperature and the time window.
The colour of the dome.

questions.explanation: A percentage change needs its starting value and period. The starting temperature and time window supply both.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Soften an absolute claim

stimulus.body: The astronomer writes: 'The dome never leaks at all.'

questions.stem: Which revision keeps the observation honest?

options.text: 'The dome stayed dry on most nights.'
'The dome never leaks at all, ever.'
'The dome is totally leak-proof.'
'The dome cannot possibly leak.'

questions.explanation: Option A replaces the absolute with a bounded, supportable claim. The others keep or inflate the overstatement.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Spot a coherence break
questions.stem: Log entry: 'The focuser slipped. I recorded the humidity. The image was sharp.' Which sentence breaks coherence?

options.text: All three cohere perfectly.
'The focuser slipped' is out of order.
'The image was sharp' is too vague.
'I recorded the humidity' lacks a link to the others.

questions.explanation: The humidity sentence appears without a stated reason or connection. Adding why it was recorded restores coherence.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Frame a quotation effectively
questions.stem: An astronomer opens a log with a quote and no explanation. What is the flaw?

options.text: Quotes are never allowed in logs.
Readers cannot tell why the quote matters.
The quote must be translated first.
The flaw is using a quote at all.

questions.explanation: A quotation needs a framing sentence to show its relevance. Without it, the entry loses its thread.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Remove redundant modifiers
questions.stem: An astronomer writes 'a very unique and totally unprecedented event.' Which words can go?

answer.exemplar: Cut 'very' and 'totally' because 'unique' and 'unprecedented' already express totality.

questions.explanation: Modifiers like 'very' and 'totally' are redundant with absolute adjectives. Removing them tightens the phrase.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Spot a nominalised process

stimulus.body: The entry says: 'The calibration of the sensor was performed by the team before dawn.'

questions.stem: Which nominalisation weakens this sentence?

options.text: 'dawn' is a poetic word.
options.misconception: word choice is not the issue

options.text: 'sensor' is too technical for a log.
'calibration' turns the verb 'calibrate' into a noun.
'team' hides individual responsibility.

questions.explanation: 'Calibration' buries the action in a noun. 'The team calibrated the sensor before dawn' is clearer and shorter.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Match voice to purpose

stimulus.body: A log written for a safety review must show who checked the mount. The draft reads: 'The mount was checked.'

questions.stem: What voice change does the safety review require?

options.text: Question form to engage readers.

Imperative mood for all sentences.
Active voice naming the checker.

questions.explanation: A safety review needs accountability, which active voice supplies by naming who checked the mount.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Judge when a hedge is justified
questions.stem: An astronomer writes 'the seeing was probably around 3 arcseconds' after measuring it twice. Is the hedge justified?

options.text: No, because any hedge shows weakness.
Yes, because measurement spread supports a qualifier.
No, because two measurements are too few.
options.misconception: two measurements can support a qualifier

options.text: Yes, because all log entries need hedges.

questions.explanation: A qualifier is justified when it reflects real measurement spread. Here two readings support 'around' rather than an exact value.
